subject: biology
title: Bacteria, Vaccines & Resistance
welcome_lead: Today you'll calculate bacterial growth, explain how vaccines work, and meet the antibiotic resistance crisis.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology Infection & Response calculations — bacterial doubling, vaccination, antibiotics and resistance.
final_note: You can now use 2ⁿ to predict bacterial numbers, explain vaccination, and say why antibiotic resistance matters.

concepts.def: Bacterial reproduction by splitting in two
Time for a bacterial population to double

Lymphocyte that remembers a past pathogen

walkthroughs.body_html:
Bacteria reproduce by binary fission — one cell splits into two.

If the doubling time is 20 minutes, then after n doublings you have N × 2ⁿ bacteria, where N is the starting number.

Example: 1 bacterium, 1 hour, doubling every 20 min → 3 doublings → 1 × 2³ = 8 bacteria.

Example: 100 bacteria, 2 hours → 6 doublings → 100 × 64 = 6,400 bacteria.

A vaccine contains a dead or weakened pathogen — safe, but it still has the antigens.

Your lymphocytes make antibodies and memory cells.

If the real pathogen invades later, memory cells make antibodies quickly and in huge numbers — you don't get ill.

If a high % of the population is vaccinated, pathogens can't spread easily. This is called herd immunity.

Antibiotics (like penicillin) kill bacteria inside your body.

They do NOT kill viruses — viruses hide inside your cells, so the drug can't reach them without damaging you too.

Random mutations can make a bacterium resistant. If you don't finish your course, resistant bacteria survive and multiply — that's how MRSA appeared.

To slow resistance: only use antibiotics when needed, and always finish the course.

Viruses live inside your own cells
Viruses don't have antigens
Viruses are killed by phagocytes only
A live, full-strength pathogen
Antibiotics
A dead or weakened pathogen
Memory cells

mcqs.q: How do vaccines protect you from a disease?
options: Vaccines kill the pathogen if it ever enters the body.
Mutations only happen in organisms that have been damaged by external chemicals.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
They expose your immune system to a harmless form of the pathogen so memory cells form, allowing rapid response if exposed later.

Prokaryotes have no DNA — that's why they have no nucleus.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Prokaryotes are always smaller than 1 micrometre and have no cytoplasm.
They are random changes in DNA — caused by errors in replication or by mutagens — not directed by need.
Mutations occur because organisms need to adapt to their environment.
